summary:
HyperLife is a smart AI-based health monitoring system. It exists to help astronauts notice health risks early in environments where gravity, radiation and isolation all work against the body.

It combines a web application with a wearable device "HyperWatch" to generate a dashboard that presents vital-sign trends, hazard risk assessments across five physiological domains, individualized recommendations, and a composite crew score for comparison between crew members.

HyperLife aims to support the Artemis program and preparation for Mars by showing that low-cost, compact devices can yield high-value data on human adaptation to spaceflight.
details:
How does it work:

the system detects five types of health risks (Cardiovascular risks, bone density loss risks, immune system change risks, inadequate nutrition risks and behavioural health risks) using both machine learning models and a wearable device. The software guides each astronaut through registration and captures baseline data and the mission environment (Moon base, Mars base, Spaceship), so every calculation is personal and context-aware.

The system consists of three main daily forms:

  • Mood questionnaire: Helps detect negative behavioural or mental health changes.
  • FoodDiary: Inspired by the ESA diet tracker, allows users to log daily meals, water intake and whether supplements were taken, to detect nutritional inadequacies.
  • General health questionnaire: Helps detect physical health risks.

Final Dashboard and AI suggestions:

Once all three questionnaires are saved, the system ends with an easy to read dashboard; it consists of vital trend charts showing how they change over time, hazard risk assessment, and a risk trend chart with color coding to ensure simplicity and clarity.

AI suggestions are also added at the bottom of the screen with up to six concrete suggestions each day, such as hydrating, exercising, contacting family, or reporting symptoms to the flight surgeon.

The system motivates users by generating a 0–100 crew score, a letter rank (S to D), and a leaderboard that allows astronauts to compare themselves with crewmates.

Wearable device “HyperWatch” :

HyperWatch turns an ESP32-S3 SuperMini + MAX30102 + TMP117 + MPU6050 + SCD30/SCD40 + SH1106 watch into a five-domain astronaut health monitor with a transparent rule engine, an int8-quantised neural network running on-device, mission context, and ten OLED pages driven by one button.

HyperWatch information: our wearable device “HyperWatch” is highly inspired by the ACHeR study, which measures astronauts’ well being and activity during Artemis missions. HyperWatch uses Biosensors to collect real-time data.

it includes a transparent rule engine that encodes the mission risk logic for five hazard areas. And a small neural network learns nonlinear interactions between physiological, environmental, and mission-context features and provides a second, independent estimate.

The user will be able to view each risk bar with its own control factors and risk status

Primary signals for each hazard:

  • Cardio: HRV, HRV, SpO₂ and temperature, profile CVD
  • Bone: mission day, gravity, exercise, age.
  • Immune: temperature + slope, sleep and radiation
  • Radiation: daily dose, cumulative dose, mission phase
  • Sleep: sleep hours, mission day, activity

A derived acute cardiac-event probability (hybrid rules + ML) and a composite mission risk index:

Accuracy scores:

The system does not diagnose users. It simply predicts possible risks so astronauts and medical teams can act on them early.

Tools and technologies:

Design: Figma

Hardware: MAX30102 sensors for measuring heart rate and SpO₂ levels, TMP117 sensors for measuring body temperature, SCD30 for measuring radiation levels, MPU6050 for acceleration and gyroscope

Machine learning: feedforward neural network (MLP), Cloudflare Workers AI, Chrome built-in LLM, Edge AI

Programming languages: Python, JavaScript, C++

Coding assistance: GitHub Copilot, Lovable, Claude code

Visuals: all visuals were generated with Lovable AI

Key Benefits:

  • Early detection of physiological decline: Combining daily self-reports with wearable vitals helps flag anomalies before they become clinically significant.
  • Enabling cost-effective science: Uses low-cost, compact devices to collect data with high scientific value on human physiology in space.
  • Low-burden data collection: Simple and gamified logging encourages adherence during long isolated missions.
  • Supporting the Artemis program and the future of long-duration spaceflight: Addresses the monitoring needs of sustained lunar surface operations as well as other hazardous space environments.
